goals: Design a warehouse layout that follows the flow of goods and cuts travel.
Use slotting to place fast-moving items close to packing.
Match storage systems and handling equipment to the products.
Choose a picking method: single-order, batch, zone or wave.
Control receiving, packing and dispatch with clear documents.
Explain how e-commerce fulfilment is different, and track warehouse KPIs and safety.

handout.intro: A warehouse is not just a roof over products. It is a flow system: every metre walked and every pallet moved costs time and money. This session shows how to design and run a warehouse that is fast, accurate and safe.

blocks.p: Goods should move in one direction: **receiving → storage → picking → packing → dispatch**. Paths should not cross more than needed.

list: **Slotting** – put fast-moving items closest to packing and dispatch. Slow movers go further away or higher up. Frequency × distance = travel cost.
**Aisle width** – narrow aisles hold more stock but need special trucks and are slower; wide aisles are faster but hold less.
**Cross-aisles** – extra aisles across the racks let pickers take short cuts.
**Seasonality** – move items when their demand changes (for example before Ramadan or summer).

callout.title: Example
callout.text: 20 products make 60% of daily picks but sit in the middle of the racks. Moving them next to packing saves each picker about 45 minutes per shift. With 40 pickers, that is **30 hours of work saved every day**.

head: System
Best for
Watch out
rows: Many different pallets; every pallet easy to reach
FIFO: pallets roll forward on rollers
Many pallets of the same item; high density
Fast-moving small items; picker stays in one place

blocks.p: Choose equipment **with** the storage system: **reach trucks** or **order pickers** for narrow aisles, **counterbalance forklifts** for open yards, **pallet jacks** for short moves, **conveyors** for steady high volume (but they are hard to change later).

**Receiving**: check quantity, condition, batch and expiry against the purchase order, and record differences on the goods received note **before the driver leaves**. Put the stock away and update the system quickly, so it is available to sell.

head: Picking method
How it works
Best for
rows: One picker, one order at a time
Pick several orders in one trip, then sort
Many small orders with common items
Each picker covers one area; orders are combined later
Release orders in groups that match truck departure times

blocks.p: **Packing** is the last check before the customer: compare items with the packing slip, choose the right box and filling, and label correctly. Too-big boxes waste space and let items move; too-small boxes crush items.

list: **Pick list** – what to pick and where.
**Packing slip** – what is in the box (for the customer).
**Dispatch / delivery note** – what left, signed by the warehouse and the driver.
**Bill of lading or waybill** – the carrier’s transport document.

blocks.p: Load in **reverse delivery order**: the first stop is loaded last. A daily dispatch log (carrier, vehicle, seal number, time, photo of each pallet) ends most disputes about short or damaged deliveries.
**Traceability** – record batch numbers at receiving and dispatch so you can trace any product back to its supplier. For food and medicines, this is required by law.

head: Traditional (B2B)
E-commerce (B2C)
rows: Each order packed and labelled for a home

list: **Each-picking** with batch or wave picking and put-walls to sort orders.
**Micro-fulfilment centres or dark stores** – small warehouses inside the city for fast delivery.
**3PL fulfilment** – many online sellers pay a third-party logistics company to store, pick, pack and ship for them.
**Returns handling** – check, re-pack, re-stock or dispose quickly; returned stock is cash.

blocks.p: In **cross-docking**, goods arrive, are sorted by destination and leave again within hours, without being stored. It saves storage and handling, but needs very good coordination: if the inbound truck is late, the outbound trucks are late too.
A **warehouse management system (WMS)** knows where every item is (aisle, rack, level) and directs each task: put-away, picking route, packing, loading. Every move is **confirmed by a scan**.

list: **Barcodes** – cheap and reliable; each item or carton is scanned one by one.
**RFID** – tags read by radio; a whole pallet can be read at once at the door.
The WMS must be **connected to the ERP**, so sales, finance and the warehouse see the same stock.

blocks.p: **Safety first**: separate people and forklifts with marked walkways, mirrors and barriers; train and certify every driver; set speed limits; keep floors clean. Safe warehouses are also faster warehouses.

head: KPI
What it shows
rows: How many lines are picked correctly
How fast received goods become available

blocks.p: Look at productivity **and** accuracy together: pushing speed alone creates errors and rework.

terms.meaning: Deciding where each item is stored, with fast movers closest to packing.
terms.example: The top 20 items moved to ground level near packing.

terms.meaning: Racking where every pallet can be reached directly.
terms.example: Standard racks with one pallet per position.

terms.meaning: A forklift designed for narrow aisles and high racks.
Picking several orders in one trip, then sorting them.
terms.example: One picker collects 12 small orders at once.

terms.meaning: Each picker works in one area; parts of an order are combined later.
terms.example: Cold room team and dry goods team.

terms.meaning: Releasing groups of orders timed to truck departures.
terms.example: The 2 p.m. wave for the 4 p.m. trucks.

terms.meaning: Moving received goods to their storage location.
terms.example: Pallets put away within 2 hours of arrival.

terms.meaning: The signed record of what left the warehouse.
terms.example: Signed by the driver at collection.

terms.meaning: Being able to follow a product’s batch from supplier to customer.
terms.example: Finding which pharmacies received batch B2471.

terms.meaning: Moving goods from inbound to outbound trucks without storing them.
terms.example: Promotion stock in Monday morning, out Monday evening.

terms.meaning: Storing, picking, packing and shipping online orders, and handling returns.
terms.example: Same-day delivery of a phone case in Doha.

terms.meaning: A small, closed-to-the-public store used only to fulfil online orders fast.
Warehouse management system: software that tracks locations and directs warehouse work.
terms.example: The WMS sends the picker the shortest route.

terms.meaning: Time from goods arriving to being available in the system.

quiz.q: Where should the fastest-moving items be stored?
options: At the back of the warehouse
quiz.why: Slotting puts fast movers where pickers travel least.

quiz.q: A warehouse stores many pallets of the same drink and wants high density. Which system fits?
quiz.why: Drive-in racking stores many pallets of one item deep, using little floor space.

quiz.q: An online shop has hundreds of small orders with the same popular items. Which picking method saves most walking?
quiz.why: Batch picking collects several orders in one trip.

options: Releasing groups of orders timed to truck departures
quiz.why: Waves link picking to the dispatch schedule.

quiz.q: When should differences in a delivery be recorded at receiving?
quiz.why: Recording them at the dock, with the driver present, gives evidence for the claim.

quiz.q: A truck has three stops: A first, then B, then C. Which goods are loaded first?
quiz.why: Load in reverse order, so the first stop’s goods are at the door.

options: Storing goods for a long time
Moving goods from inbound to outbound trucks without storing them
quiz.why: Goods are sorted and sent on within hours.

quiz.q: How is e-commerce fulfilment different from supplying shops?
options: Many small orders, fast delivery and many returns
quiz.why: Online orders are small and many, customers expect speed, and returns are common.

quiz.q: What can RFID do that a barcode cannot?
options: Read many tagged items at once without line of sight
quiz.why: RFID tags are read by radio, so a whole pallet can be read at the door.

quiz.q: A warehouse raises picking speed from 60 to 80 lines per hour, but accuracy falls to 95%. What is the problem?
options: Speed without accuracy creates errors, returns and rework
quiz.why: Look at productivity and accuracy together.
